subject: Post-call: Performance SLOs & Autoscaling - FastPay
messages:
From: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@fastpay.com>

Cc: David Kim <david_kim@redwood.com>

Subject: Post-call: Performance SLOs & Autoscaling - FastPay

Thanks again for the call this morning — really helpful to see how Redwood thinks about autoscale + warm pools. Quick recap from our side and a couple of clarifying questions so your SEs can size things for the PoC: 

Key targets/requirements from FastPay:
- P95 latency (end-to-end) target: < 250 ms for non-batched streaming responses; first-byte (stream start) ideally < 100 ms.
- Steady throughput: ~500 requests/sec across our primary endpoint (payments reconciliation).
- Peak bursts: short spikes up to ~1,200 req/sec (bursts ~1-3 minutes).
- Concurrency: up to 50 concurrent streaming sessions per client instance; typical global concurrency ~2,000.
- Streaming behavior: we rely on token-by-token streaming and expect 1-2 partial tokens within 50-100 ms after request accepted.
- SLA expectations: 99.9% uptime for production, and predictable latency during bursts is critical.

Questions we asked you to confirm: 
1) What warm-pool sizing do you recommend to hit the 90-100s scale-up SLO for 1,200 req/sec bursts?
2) If we start from zero warm GPUs (cold), what realistic cold-start scale-up time should we expect?
3) Queueing/backpressure behavior: how does Redwood handle queue depth during a burst, and how will that affect p95?

I've attached our synthetic load profile (fastpay_load_profile.csv) and a short sketch of traffic patterns by region.

Next steps: can you share a proposed autoscale config + a short checklist for SLO qualification? Happy to set a follow-up with your SEs — Priya and I are available Thu-Fri afternoon PST.

Thanks,
Alex Johnson
Director of Engineering, FastPay
alex.johnson@fastpay.com

Subject: Re: Post-call: Performance SLOs & Autoscaling - FastPay

Alex — thanks for the clear recap and for the load CSV. Appreciate the details; this helps a lot. High level recap and our proposed next steps below.

High-level proposal (short):
- Dedicated pool with warm instances sized to absorb short (1-3 min) bursts. For the traffic you shared (steady 500 rps, 1,200 peak), our initial recommendation is a warm pool of ~5 GPU nodes (N5g equivalent) per region with autoscale to add up to +15 GPUs on burst. This assumes model parallel/quant profile similar to the models we demoed.
- Warm-pool behavior: warm nodes kept in standby (low power/hot caches) so they can accept traffic in ~30-60s for scheduling + model warm cache priming.
- Cold-starts: provisioning new GPU capacity from cloud typically adds 4-7 minutes depending on region; we treat that as fallback capacity only.
- Queueing/backpressure: we recommend a per-endpoint queue with a max depth of 200 requests and circuit-breaker at ~400ms queue wait — beyond that we can return a retry-after header or fallback to smaller model variant.

Immediate next steps: 
1) David (SE) to validate sizing assumptions and share a short SLO qualification checklist (we've attached a starter checklist).
2) Proposed follow-up: 60-min SE deep-dive + load-test plan to validate p95 targets and streaming latencies (Thu 3/24 or Fri 3/25 afternoon PST).
3) We will prepare an architecture diagram and a sample autoscale policy + tuning guide.

I've attached a short SLO qualification checklist to guide the SE call. I'll also share an architecture diagram once David confirms the sizing.

Thanks — looking forward to the SE session.

Best,
Marissa Cole

Alex / team — quick technical clarifications + what we'll validate on the SE call. TL;DR: targets are achievable, but we need to tune warm-pool sizing, batching, and queueing.

Clarifications / technical notes:
- First-byte streaming latency: achieving <100 ms first byte consistently requires TCP+TLS handshake warm paths and pre-warmed KV caches — that's exactly what warm pools solve. With a warm pool of 5 GPUs per region we expect to hit first-byte < 100 ms for most requests.
- Burst absorb: 1,200 rps spike for ~1-3 minutes: we recommend configuring headroom (concurrency slots) and client-side rate limiting. Warm pool sizing rule-of-thumb: estimate average QPS per GPU for your model/sequence length and multiply by target spike. We'll run microbenchmarks during the PoC to refine.
- Cold-starts: cold provisioning (no warm instances) in cloud ranges 4-8 minutes (image pull, model load). For SLOs, treat cold as out-of-SLO fallback.
- Queueing behavior: Redwood uses a per-route request queue with LIFO for streaming endpoints to prioritize recent interactive requests. Default max queue depth: 200. When queue latency > 250 ms we recommend returning 429 with Retry-After; alternatively pre-configured fallback to lower-cost model variant so clients still get answers within SLO.
- Autoscale timing: scaling decision loop runs at ~10s intervals. When a scale event is triggered we have two timelines: (a) warm-pool allocate: if nodes exist in warm pool, scheduling+cache-priming ≈ 30-60s; (b) cold-provision: spinning new nodes from cloud ≈ 4-7 minutes. We'll show numbers from our benchmarks on the call.
- Warm-pool sizing exercise (quick math): if your model yields ~25 rps per GPU at target latency, to absorb an extra 700 rps burst you need ~28 GPUs of headroom. That suggests either a larger warm pool or a small warm pool combined with very aggressive autoscale + brief queuing. We'll validate with your exact model/seq-length.

Action items for SE call:
- We'll run a baseline microbenchmark with a representative model and your sample payloads.
- Validate exact rps/GPU and streaming throughput to size warm pool correctly.
- Provide recommended autoscale policy (scale-out thresholds, cool-downs, max queue depth) and a runbook for failing over to fallback variants.

I'll attach the Redwood architecture diagram and a sample autoscale policy in the follow-up email. Looking forward to the deep dive.

-David
David Kim
